column1: # What it would take to detect a technique that MITRE says shows up in network
# traffic and that has no detection here. Printed beside the technique in the
# coverage report's list of gaps. A note for a technique that is covered is ignored.

column2: note
The command that puts a device into firmware update mode is different for each vendor; a rule needs a capture of each one.
Shows as steady reading from an address that does not normally read. The three OT anomaly detectors (shipped switched off) are the nearest thing; there is no rule.
Web browsing from the control network. The general rule set bundled with the product is where exploit-kit rules live; it is not counted on this page.
Exploits of known vulnerabilities are in the general rule set bundled with the product, listed by CVE in the build's vulnerability coverage report; they are not counted on this page.
Writes to alarm limits look like any other write unless the sensor is told which points hold alarm settings. Only DNP3's switch for unsolicited reporting is watched.
Needs the list of real masters. Set MODBUS_CLIENT and DNP3_CLIENT on the sensor and the imported Quickdraw rules name commands from any other address.
Radio links are not on the wire the sensor listens to.
A new laptop on the network appears in the product's asset inventory; no alert is defined for it here.
Email is not normally carried on a control network; this belongs to the mail gateway.
Operator stations read the controller's mode all day. A rule needs the list of stations allowed to ask.
Proxy and tunnelling tools have nothing specific to industrial networks to match on; the general rule set is where such rules belong.
The imported Quickdraw set has rules for another protocol on the Modbus and DNP3 ports. Nothing in this repository does it.

RDP, SSH and file sharing inside the network are normal engineering traffic; they become a signal only against a record of who normally uses them. The correlation rules use remote access from outside as their first step.
Radio links are not on the wire the sensor listens to.
Password-change commands are different for each vendor; a rule needs a capture of each one.
A blocked command shows as traffic that stops. That needs a baseline of what is expected, which rules do not have.
A false report cannot be told from a true one without knowing the real process value. Reports from an address that is not the device could be caught with a list of devices.
On most protocols a module's firmware arrives the same way as the device's own; the rules here cannot tell them apart.
Default and hardcoded passwords can be matched where logins are not encrypted (Telnet, FTP, plain HTTP), one product at a time. The imported ELITEWOLF set does it for SEL relays.
Default passwords can be matched where logins are not encrypted, one product at a time. The imported ELITEWOLF set does it for SEL relays.
Hardcoded passwords can be matched where logins are not encrypted, one product at a time. Nothing here does.

The serial link itself is not on the Ethernet the sensor listens to. MITRE's example is a TCP session held open to the serial-to-Ethernet converter so nothing else can use it; catching that needs the list of converters and the addresses allowed to connect to them.
Radio links are not on the wire the sensor listens to.
The layer 2 watch detects ARP poisoning. If this page lists the technique as a gap, the build left the watch out: out/rule-check.txt says why.
